title: After a consulting rejection, ask for feedback, fix the one or two real gaps and plan your next attempt
description: A kind, practical guide to handling a rejection from a consulting firm: getting useful feedback, deciding what to work on, and when to apply again.
hook: If you have just been rejected, I am sorry. It hurts, especially after weeks of preparation. Please know that consulting interviews are hard, places are limited, and many people who now work at top firms were rejected at least once along the way. A rejection is information, not a verdict on you. Here is how to use it.
body:
Give yourself a day

Feel disappointed. Talk to someone. You do not need to analyse anything on the same day.

Ask for feedback

Many firms will share some feedback if you ask politely, especially after final rounds. Keep it short: thank them, say you would value any feedback to help you improve, and ask which areas to focus on. Then listen without arguing.

Find the real pattern

Look back honestly across your interviews and practice cases. Was it structure, maths, driving the case, the recommendation, or the fit interview? Usually one or two areas explain most of the result. This list of common mistakes can help you name it.

Make a focused plan

Fix the specific weakness rather than doing more of everything. If maths let you down, do short daily maths for a month. If you struggled to drive the case, do cases where your partner tallies every time you wait to be told what to do.

Applying again

Firms often allow you to reapply after a set period, commonly a year or so; check each firm's policy. Other firms may have different timelines, so a rejection from one does not close the others. When you reapply, being able to show how you have grown since is a real strength.

Keep perspective

Consulting is one path among many. The skills you have built, structured thinking, clear communication and business sense, are valuable wherever you go next.
outro: Read it once, then try it on a practice case today while it is fresh. One real attempt teaches more than three re-reads.
